answer:
A 2026 Clinical Nutrition trial concluded that time-restricted eating “was not more beneficial with regard to reduction in body weight than daily calorie restriction” [2]. In that trial, the difference between groups was 1.8 kg and was not statistically significant [2].

An Annals of Internal Medicine trial published in the May 20, 2025 issue found that after one year, the 4:3 fasting group lost an average of about 6 more pounds than the calorie-restriction group [1]. That trial involved 165 people with an average age of 42 [1]. The 4:3 group ate 20% of usual calories on fasting days, while the other group reduced daily calories by 34% [1]. A 2025 report on the same Annals trial says 4:3 fasting outperformed daily caloric restriction by 2.89 kg, a statistically significant difference [3].

For the 16:8 format, a 2023 meta-analysis in Nutrients of seven randomized trials with 458 participants found time-restricted eating combined with a calorie deficit produced 2.11 kg more weight loss than calorie restriction alone [3]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 11 trials with 705 participants reported a small but statistically significant weight-loss advantage for fasting, while BMI outcomes were essentially identical [3]. A recent review found that intermittent fasting produced as much weight loss as calorie restriction overall, though alternate-day fasting seemed to lead to greater weight loss [4].
